strengths: Addresses a genuine practical bottleneck in indoor 3D occupancy prediction: the small size and privacy sensitivity of existing labeled indoor datasets (e.g., NYUv2 with only 1,449 images). Using freely available YouTube house-tour videos as a scalable data source is a novel and useful idea for the community.

The fully automated data pipeline (clip segmentation, outdoor-scene filtering, Dust3R-based camera/depth estimation, point-cloud cleaning and re-scaling, VFM-based semantic labeling, voxelization) is well described and demonstrates that camera-parameter-free 3D reconstruction can be bootstrapped from in-the-wild video, which is a nontrivial engineering and methodological contribution.

The proposed superpixel/supervoxel contrastive distillation is architecture-agnostic and conceptually well-motivated: grouping pixels/voxels at the object level (via VFM masks) avoids the pitfalls of naive pixel/voxel-level contrastive losses under scale variation and occlusion common in indoor scenes.

Experiments span multiple axes: full-annotation comparison against strong baselines on NYUv2 and OccScanNet, annotation-efficiency curves at multiple label percentages, cross-dataset pre-training with YouTube-Occ, and a zero-shot transfer setting, giving a reasonably thorough picture of when the pre-training helps most (which appears to be in the low-annotation regime).

The paper is generally clearly written, with a logical structure and figures/tables that support the narrative, and the checklist and implementation details (optimizer, epochs, hardware) support partial reproducibility of the training procedure.
weaknesses: The improvements at full annotation are numerically small (e.g., +0.30% mIoU / +0.25% IoU on OccScanNet, +1.04% mIoU on NYUv2), and no statistical significance or repeated-run variance is reported, making it hard to judge whether the gains are meaningful versus noise.

The YouTube-Occ dataset — the paper's central contribution — will not be publicly released, which substantially limits reproducibility and community benefit; for a paper that leans heavily on the value of a new dataset/pipeline, withholding the data undercuts the practical impact and verifiability of the claims.

The abstract claims 'state-of-the-art zero-shot performance,' but Table 5 reports only the proposed method's own zero-shot numbers (9.95% mIoU on NYUv2, 4.61% on OccScanNet) with no comparison to any other zero-shot baseline, so the 'state-of-the-art' framing is not substantiated and appears overstated relative to the (quite low) absolute numbers shown.

No ablation studies isolating the contribution of individual pipeline components (e.g., superpixel granularity/VFM choice, effect of the point-cloud filtering steps, sensitivity to the heuristic 2.8m wall-height metric scaling, choice of Dust3R vs. alternatives) are provided, making it difficult to assess which parts of the pipeline actually drive the reported gains.
All experiments use a single occupancy backbone (Symphonies); the claim that the pre-training method is 'model-agnostic' is not empirically verified with a second architecture.

The semantic pseudo-labels used for both the YouTube-Occ dataset and the distillation targets come from off-the-shelf VFMs (SAN, DINOv2) whose noise/error characteristics on real estate video frames are not quantified, so the quality and reliability of the underlying supervision signal remains unverified.

The scale-normalization heuristic (assuming a fixed 2.8m wall height) is a strong and somewhat fragile assumption for metric-scale recovery from monocular reconstruction across diverse real-world houses, and its impact on downstream geometric accuracy is not analyzed.

Real estate/house-tour videos may capture private property interiors and personal belongings; while the dataset is not released, the underlying data collection and its ethical/privacy handling (e.g., consent, uploader terms) could be discussed more thoroughly given the emphasis on privacy motivation in the introduction.

strengths: Novel, well-motivated data-centric contribution: the paper is (to the reviewer's knowledge) the first to explore learning indoor 3D semantic occupancy from unlabeled, uncalibrated in-the-wild internet videos, directly addressing a genuine bottleneck (scarcity and cost of annotated indoor 3D data) in the field.

The automated data curation pipeline is sensible and clearly described, combining modern 3D foundation models (Dust3R) for geometry/point-cloud reconstruction with 2D open-vocabulary segmentation (SAN) for semantic pseudo-labeling, along with practical post-processing (z-up alignment, metric-scale normalization) to make raw web video usable for occupancy voxelization.

The paper honestly reports a negative result (naive supervision with pseudo-labels fails or even hurts performance) and uses this finding to motivate the proposed pre-training framework, which strengthens the scientific narrative rather than overselling the straightforward pipeline.

The dual-alignment pre-training framework (intra-frame region contrastive loss via voxel-anchored Gaussian rendering + cross-scene class-prototype distillation) is a reasonable and moderately novel adaptation of image-to-LiDAR/outdoor distillation ideas to the indoor, uncalibrated setting, and is explicitly designed to be model-agnostic.

Experimental evaluation is fairly extensive: three distinct occupancy architectures (CNN, voxel-transformer, Gaussian-transformer), two standard benchmarks (NYUv2, Occ-ScanNet), few-shot/data-efficiency experiments, comparisons against alternative auxiliary-loss and pre-training baselines (HASSC, GaussRender, Pri3D), and ablations isolating the contribution of each loss term and design choice (Gaussianization vs. direct projection, prototype momentum).

Reported gains are consistent (not just on a single architecture/dataset) and, importantly, are more substantial in low-label/few-shot regimes, which is the practically relevant setting the paper targets and supports the core claim that web video pre-training aids data efficiency.
Plan to release code and data would aid reproducibility and could benefit the community given the stated novelty of the data source and pipeline.
weaknesses: Absolute performance gains from the full pre-training framework are relatively modest in the full-data regime (roughly +1-2% mIoU across architectures/datasets), which somewhat tempers the practical significance despite the added pipeline and training complexity; the paper would benefit from clearer discussion of when the added complexity is/isn't worth it.

The metric-scale normalization relies on a fixed 2.8 m wall-height heuristic, which is a strong and somewhat brittle assumption (acknowledged as a limitation) but its sensitivity/impact on downstream results is not empirically probed (e.g., how errors in this assumption propagate to occupancy quality).

The web-video source is restricted to real-estate channel footage, which, while practically justified (stability, indoor content, static scenes), is a fairly narrow and stylistically homogeneous slice of "in-the-wild" video; broader diversity (e.g., handheld consumer footage, varied lighting/clutter) is not explored, limiting claims about generalization to truly unconstrained web video.

Pseudo-label quality is only assessed qualitatively (Fig. 4) and indirectly through downstream training performance (Table 1); a more direct quantitative analysis of pseudo-label geometric/semantic accuracy (e.g., against ScanNet ground truth or other proxy metrics) would strengthen confidence in the pipeline's reliability and help explain why naive supervision fails.

Some baseline comparisons (e.g., Pri3D underperforming the vanilla baseline) raise questions about whether these competing methods were adequately tuned or adapted for the indoor/occupancy setting, and more implementation detail would help readers judge the fairness of these comparisons.

There is limited discussion of computational/pipeline overhead (e.g., cost of running Dust3R + SAN at scale for 100K+ frames) relative to the modest performance gains, which is relevant for assessing the practical trade-offs of this data-centric approach.

Licensing/ethical considerations of scraping and redistributing YouTube-derived reconstructions and pseudo-labels for a public dataset release are not discussed, which is a relevant consideration given the paper's emphasis on privacy-sensitive indoor data.
